vignette:
Marcus

Marcus sits in the office with his shoulders slightly hunched, fingers fidgeting with the zipper on his hoodie. At twenty-four, he has the lean frame of someone who hasn't been eating quite right, and there are dark circles under his eyes that suggest sleep hasn't come easily in months. He works as a QA engineer at a mid-sized software company downtown—a job he'd been excited about when he started two years ago. Now, he describes it as something he does on autopilot, though lately even that feels impossible.

The story unfolds slowly. Fourteen months ago, Marcus was at the Riverside Event Center for a concert with friends. He'd been looking forward to it for weeks—a chance to unwind after a brutal sprint at work. The venue was packed, maybe three thousand people, and the energy was electric. He remembers the opening act clearly, remembers texting his mother that he was having a good time. Then, somewhere between the second and third song, the structure failed. A section of the upper mezzanine collapsed without warning.

Marcus doesn't talk about the collapse itself in clinical terms. Instead, he describes the sound—a noise he says he'll never unhear, a combination of metal screaming and people screaming that he now hears in his sleep. He was on the main floor, far enough away to survive, but close enough to see the aftermath. He remembers the dust, the sudden chaos, people running in all directions. He remembers helping pull someone out from under debris, remembers the weight of a stranger's arm across his shoulders as they stumbled toward the exit. Thirty-seven people died that day.

In the weeks after, Marcus functioned. He went to work, attended the funerals of two people he knew peripherally, gave a statement to investigators. But somewhere around week three, the functionality started to crack. He began having panic attacks at his desk—sudden, overwhelming surges of fear that would send him to the bathroom to collect himself. His manager noticed his productivity dropping. Code reviews that used to take him an hour now took three because he couldn't concentrate. He'd read the same line of code five times without absorbing it.

Sleep became a battleground. When he closed his eyes, he was back there—the sound, the dust, the specific weight of that stranger's arm. He started staying up later, scrolling through his phone until exhaustion forced him under. Even then, he'd wake at three or four in the morning with his heart racing, sheets soaked with sweat. On bad nights, he'd lie awake until dawn, too afraid to sleep.

The hypervigilance crept in gradually. He finds himself scanning crowds now, noting exits, calculating escape routes. At the office, he sits with his back to the wall. When his coworkers laugh loudly nearby, his entire body tenses. He's become withdrawn—his friends have noticed he declines most invitations, and the few times he's tried to go out, he's had to leave early. Even being in his apartment building's lobby makes him anxious. Crowds feel dangerous in a way they never did before.

What troubles Marcus most is the sense that he's changed fundamentally. He doesn't recognize himself anymore. The person who loved live music, who went to concerts and festivals, who was easy to be around—that person feels like someone else entirely. Now he's someone who jumps at loud noises, who can't sit through a movie without scanning for exits, who lies awake at night replaying moments he can't change. He's still going to work, still showing up, but he's not sure how much longer he can keep pretending everything is fine.
